words.definition: The use of machines and computers to do work that was previously done by people.
words.example: Automation threatens to displace millions of workers in manufacturing, retail and logistics.

words.definition: No longer used or useful because something newer and better has replaced it.
words.example: Many skills that were once highly valued have been rendered obsolete by technological advances.

words.definition: The gap between people who have easy access to computers and the internet and people who do not.
words.example: Unless the digital divide is addressed, the shift to online learning will only widen existing educational inequalities.

words.definition: The most modern and advanced of its kind.
words.example: Countries that invest in cutting-edge research tend to attract highly skilled workers and foreign investment.

words.definition: The right of people to control how their personal information is collected, stored and used.
words.example: Many users willingly sacrifice their data privacy in exchange for the convenience of free online services.

words.definition: The careful watching of people, often by the state or the police, to gather information or prevent crime.
words.example: The widespread use of facial recognition cameras raises serious questions about state surveillance and civil liberties.

words.definition: The amount of time a person spends using a device with a screen, such as a phone, computer or television.
words.example: Paediatricians recommend limiting children's screen time to protect their sleep and concentration.

words.definition: Knowing a lot about modern technology and confident in using it.
words.example: While younger generations are generally tech-savvy, many elderly people struggle to access public services that have moved online.

words.definition: Describing a new product or technology that completely changes the way an industry works.
words.example: Ride-hailing apps proved highly disruptive to the traditional taxi industry within just a few years.

words.definition: Something that has both clear advantages and clear disadvantages.
words.example: Social media is a double-edged sword: it connects people across continents but can also fuel isolation and anxiety.
collocations: prove to be a double-edged sword

words.definition: Too much dependence on something, so that you cannot manage without it.
words.example: An over-reliance on satellite navigation may gradually erode people's natural sense of direction.

words.definition: The protection of computer systems, networks and data from attack, damage or theft.
words.example: As power grids and hospitals move online, investment in cybersecurity has become a matter of national security.

words.definition: To control and use something, such as a resource or an idea, in order to produce benefits.
words.example: If harnessed responsibly, artificial intelligence could transform the diagnosis and treatment of disease.

words.definition: At a very early stage of development.
words.example: Although driverless car technology is still in its infancy, it could eventually make roads far safer.

words.definition: Never having happened or existed before, or never to this degree.
words.example: The internet has given ordinary citizens unprecedented access to information and expertise.

words.definition: Seeming to be everywhere at the same time; extremely common.
words.example: Smartphones have become so ubiquitous that it is difficult to imagine daily life without them.
